record.title: PaperFormalizer preprint reports author-approved repairs to proof gaps in three research papers
record.summary: A Stanford-authored preprint introduces PaperFormalizer, a coding-agent pipeline that transcribes research statements, checks them for ambiguity and correctness, asks authors to decide claim-changing repairs, and formalizes reviewed results in Lean. The authors report using it on three of their papers: in a treatment-effects paper, five of seven results were false as printed and repaired with author approval; all seven revised results were then proved in Lean without `sorry` or axioms beyond Lean's standard ones. They report that 15 of 29 results needed revision in a second paper, while all 12 results in an optimal-transport paper were proved as printed. These are author-reported case studies, not an independent error rate or evidence of general accuracy.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The Oct 26 arXiv announcement presents PaperFormalizer as an author-in-the-loop coding-agent workflow that reviews paper statements, requests author decisions on claim-changing repairs, and produces linked Lean formalizations.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors' treatment-effects case study, they report that five of seven results were false as printed and repaired with author approval, after which all seven revised results were proved in Lean without `sorry` or axioms beyond Lean's standard ones.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that 15 of 29 results needed revision in a second paper and that all 12 results in a third, optimal-transport paper were proved as printed.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The preprint does not establish an independent error-detection rate, generalization to other authors' papers, comparative time or model cost, or broader adoption; the paper-specific shared artifacts were not independently inspected in this activation.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper-specific Lean toolkit and shared run artifact were not independently retrieved, and no external reproduction was performed.
Three author papers do not establish how often the workflow finds real proof errors or how well it works for unrelated authors and domains.

brief.importance_rationale: If the author-controlled pipeline generalizes, identifying unstated assumptions and proof errors while preserving author decisions could improve mathematical reliability and reduce the effort needed to formalize research. Importance is 6 because the paper reports substantive errors and repairs in three case studies, but all outcome evidence is author-reported and general effectiveness is unknown.
limitations: All three case-study outcomes are reported by the paper's authors; no independent reproduction was run.
The detailed treatment-effects example is one author-selected paper; the counts are not an estimate of prevalence or a general detection rate.
The public pipeline repository was inspected, but the paper-specific Lean toolkit, run log and shared-paper artifact were not independently retrieved.
No matched baseline, end-to-end time, model-token cost or independent-author adoption measure is reported here.

The arXiv abstract history lists author upload on Oct 22; the public new-submissions listing is dated Oct 26. This record uses the public announcement date for event recency and preserves the earlier upload time in the source locator.
brief.summary: A Stanford-authored preprint introduces PaperFormalizer, a coding-agent pipeline that transcribes research statements, checks them for ambiguity and correctness, asks authors to decide claim-changing repairs, and formalizes reviewed results in Lean. The authors report using it on three of their papers: in a treatment-effects paper, five of seven results were false as printed and repaired with author approval; all seven revised results were then proved in Lean without `sorry` or axioms beyond Lean's standard ones. They report that 15 of 29 results needed revision in a second paper, while all 12 results in an optimal-transport paper were proved as printed. technical.claimed_result: The authors report finding and repairing five of seven false-as-printed results in one treatment-effects paper, formalizing all seven revised results, revising 15 of 29 results in a second paper, and formalizing all 12 results in a third paper.
technical.compute_or_cost: The repository README says a Mathlib-only toolkit uses about 8 GB and a full run is long and token-heavy; it gives no measured cost for the reported case studies.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint describes the pipeline and reports these case studies; this activation did not independently validate the reported theorem repairs or rebuild the paper-specific Lean artifacts.
technical.mechanism: A coding-agent pipeline converts a paper into a dependency graph, reviews statements for fidelity/ambiguity/correctness, proposes repairs, pauses for author decisions when a repair could change a claim, and proves reviewed statements in Lean with links back to the paper.
technical.novelty: The contribution is an end-to-end author-controlled workflow joining natural-language statement review, repair decisions, Lean proof construction and paper-to-code links; related automatic formalization systems are discussed in the paper.
technical.regime: Author-in-the-loop mathematical paper review and Lean formalization, demonstrated by the authors on three of their own research papers.
technical.strongest_baseline: No matched baseline or comparison against expert-only review or another formalization workflow is reported in this bounded account.

brief.title: PaperFormalizer preprint reports author-approved repairs to proof gaps in three research papers
brief.why_it_matters: The case study reports material proof and assumption gaps in published research and demonstrates a workflow that keeps authors responsible for changes to what a theorem claims. If the approach generalizes, it could make formal verification more usable in research practice. The reported cases are selected from the authors' own papers; independent reproduction, general effectiveness, time and token cost, and uptake beyond the authors are not established.
